read.sections.0.heading.source: New machines have changed work before
read.sections.0.heading.back: New machines have changed jobs before

read.sections.0.text.source: AI is not the first technology to change people's work. In England in the early 1800s, new machines in cloth factories began to do work that skilled cloth workers had done by hand. Between 1811 and 1816, some of these workers, known as Luddites, broke machines in protest, because the machines were taking their work. Much later, from the 1970s, cash machines slowly spread to banks in the United States. Many people expected bank tellers, who handle money at the counter, to disappear. Instead, a study from 2015 found that the number of tellers stayed about the same and even grew a little. Each branch needed fewer tellers, so banks could open more branches. Tellers spent less time counting cash and more time helping customers. That was one machine in one country, so it can't tell us what AI will do.
read.sections.0.text.back: AI is not the first technology to change people's jobs. In England shortly after 1800, new machines in cloth factories began doing work skilled weavers had done by hand. Between 1811 and 1816 a group of workers called Luddites smashed machines in protest because the machines were taking their jobs. Much later, from the 1970s, cash machines slowly spread through banks in the United States. Many expected that bank tellers, who handle money at the counter, would disappear. But a 2015 study found the number of tellers stayed about the same and even rose a little. Each branch needed fewer staff, so banks could open more branches. Tellers spent less time counting cash and more time helping customers. That was one kind of machine in one country, so it cannot tell us what AI will do.
read.sections.0.text.note: Luddites = ลัดไดต์ in Thai script (the checker warns that the Latin name is missing; expected). "early 1800s" = ช่วงหลังปี 1800 ไม่นาน ("shortly after 1800"), and the simpler "1800s" = ช่วงปี 1800 ถึง 1899 per KEY_TERMS. bank tellers = พนักงานรับฝากถอนเงิน; cash machines = ตู้กดเงิน.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: AI is not the first technology to change work. In the 1800s, new machines in England did the work of skilled cloth workers. Some workers, called Luddites, broke machines in protest. From the 1970s, banks in the United States got cash machines. Many thought bank workers at the counter would disappear. But a 2015 study found there were still about as many. Banks opened more branches. The workers counted less cash and helped customers more. That was one machine in one country. It can't tell us what AI will do.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: AI is not the first technology to change jobs. In the 1800s new machines in England did the work of skilled weavers. Some workers called Luddites smashed machines in protest. From the 1970s banks in the United States had cash machines. Many people thought bank counter staff would disappear. But a 2015 study found there were still about as many staff as before. Banks opened more branches. Staff counted less money and helped customers more. That was one kind of machine in one country. It cannot tell what AI will do.

read.sections.1.heading.back: AI changes the tasks in each job

read.sections.1.text.source: Most jobs are made of many tasks. A new technology may automate some tasks, but not the whole job. When spreadsheets came to office computers in the United States, many bookkeepers lost their work, but the number of accountants grew. In 2025, the ILO, the United Nations agency for work, studied AI tools that write and make things. Its researchers scored about 30,000 tasks for how much of each one these tools could do. They found that about one in four of the world's jobs has some exposure to these tools. Office jobs, such as clerks who type in data, have the most. Exposure tells us what the tools could do. It is not a count of jobs lost. The ILO says most of these jobs are more likely to change than to disappear, because people are still needed for many tasks.
read.sections.1.text.back: Most jobs are made up of many tasks. A new technology may automate some tasks but not the whole job. When spreadsheet programs arrived on office computers in the United States, many bookkeepers lost their jobs but the number of accountants grew. In 2025 the ILO, the United Nations agency for labour, studied AI tools that can write and create things. ILO researchers scored about 30,000 tasks on how much these tools could do each one. They found about a quarter of the world's jobs have some exposure to these tools. Office jobs, such as clerks who type data into computers, have the most exposure. Exposure tells us what tools can do, but not the number of jobs lost. The ILO says most of these jobs are more likely to change than to disappear, because many tasks still need people.
read.sections.1.text.note: spreadsheets = โปรแกรมตารางคำนวณ; bookkeepers = พนักงานทำบัญชี, accountants = นักบัญชี. ILO kept as Latin and explained once as หน่วยงานของสหประชาชาติด้านแรงงาน.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: A job is made of many tasks. A new technology may automate some tasks, not the whole job. Spreadsheets did sums for office workers. Some people who added up numbers lost their work. But there were more accountants. In 2025, a United Nations group for work studied AI that writes and makes things. It checked about 30,000 tasks. About one in four jobs has some exposure to these tools. That means the tools could do some of the tasks. Office jobs have the most. This is not a count of lost jobs. Most of these jobs will likely change, not disappear.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: A job is made of many tasks. A new technology may automate some tasks, but not the whole job. Spreadsheet programs did sums for office workers. Some people who used to add up numbers lost their jobs, but there came to be more accountants. In 2025 the United Nations' labour agency studied AI that can write and create things. It checked about 30,000 tasks. About a quarter of jobs have some exposure to these tools. That means the tools might do some tasks. Office jobs have the most exposure. This is not the number of jobs lost. Most of these jobs will probably change, not disappear.

read.sections.2.text.source: The same change can affect people very differently. The ILO found that exposure is higher in richer countries: about one in three jobs, against about one in ten in the poorest countries. In richer countries, more of women's jobs than men's are in the most exposed group. Change can be uneven inside one office too. In the made-up town of Millbrook, the water office now works faster. After training, two clerks moved to the help desk, but the third lost her work. The ILO says talks between workers, employers and governments can help to manage these changes. Who gains depends partly on the choices people make.
read.sections.2.text.back: The same change can affect people very differently. The ILO found exposure is higher in richer countries, about a third of jobs, compared with about a tenth in the poorest countries. In richer countries a higher share of women's jobs than men's jobs are in the most exposed group. Change can be uneven even within one office. In Millbrook, a fictional town, the water office now works faster. After training two clerks moved to the help desk, but the third lost her job. The ILO says talks between workers, employers and governments can help manage these changes. So who gains depends partly on the choices people make.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: Change can affect people in different ways. The ILO found more exposure in richer countries. There, about one in three jobs has some. In the poorest countries, it is about one in ten. In richer countries, more women's jobs than men's are very exposed. In made-up Millbrook, the water office works faster now. After training, two clerks moved to the help desk. The third clerk lost her work. Workers, employers and leaders can plan these changes together, the ILO says.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: Change can affect people differently. The ILO found richer countries have more exposure. There about a third of jobs have some exposure. In the poorest countries it is about a tenth. In richer countries there are more highly exposed women's jobs than men's. In Millbrook, a fictional town, the water office now works faster. write.example.source: I chose the clerks at the Millbrook water office. The task that changed was typing up forms, because an AI tool now reads most of them. The office gained, because the work is faster. Ines gained too, because after training she moved to the help desk. The third clerk lost her work. This is like the bank tellers, because Ines's work moved towards helping people. It is also unlike them, because one clerk lost her job, while the number of tellers did not fall.
write.example.back: I chose the clerks at the water office in Millbrook. The task that changed is typing forms, because now an AI tool reads most forms. The office gained, because work is faster. Ines gained too, because after training she moved to the help desk. The third clerk lost her job. This is like the bank tellers, because Ines's work changed to helping people. But it is also different, because one clerk lost her job, while the number of bank tellers did not fall.

watch.beforeQuestion.source: Do you think new machines make more jobs or fewer jobs? Why?

watch.afterQuestion.source: Why does the video say that who gains from technology depends on people's choices?

watch.summary.source: This video asks if machines and AI will take away people's jobs. People have worried about this many times before. In the United States, machines replaced many workers in the 1920s and 1930s. It happened again around 1960. Machines took work on farms, in factories and on telephone lines. But most people still found work. Technology makes some new jobs, such as building and fixing machines. It also makes things cheaper. Then people spend money on other things, like haircuts or eating out, and those need workers too. Some experts say AI is different, because it can do many kinds of work. The video says the bigger question may be who gains. The gains from technology have not been shared fairly. The rules people choose can change that.
watch.summary.back: This video asks whether machines and AI will take people's jobs. People have worried about this many times. In the United States machines replaced many workers in the 1920s and 1930s, and again around 1960. Machines came to work on farms, in factories and on telephone lines, but most people still found work. Technology created some new jobs, such as building and fixing machines. It also made things cheaper, and then people spent money on other things, such as haircuts or eating out, which also need workers. Some experts say AI is different because it can do many kinds of work. The video says the bigger question may be who gains. The gains from technology have not been shared fairly. The rules people choose can change this.

educatorNotes.0.source: One estimate in learner text, on purpose: the ILO's Generative AI and jobs, a 2025 update (Gmyrek and others, 20 May 2025, with Poland's NASK; ILO Working Paper 140). It scored nearly 30,000 tasks for how far generative AI could do them. 25% of the world's jobs are in occupations with some exposure (34% in high-income countries, 11% in low-income ones); 3.3% are in the most exposed group, mostly clerical jobs such as data entry clerks and typists; in high-income countries that group is 9.6% of women's jobs and 3.5% of men's. The ILO says the figures reflect potential exposure, an upper limit, not the actual effect on employment; it expects most jobs to be transformed rather than made redundant, though efficiency gains could still reduce demand for workers. Other estimates, such as the IMF's (January 2024: almost 40% of jobs exposed to AI in general), cover a wider set of technologies and use another method, so they can't be set beside the ILO's number; the lesson uses only the ILO's. The bank teller example is US data from the 1970s to the 2000s (James Bessen, 2015), and the spreadsheet example is from NPR (2015); each is one past case, not a forecast for AI.
educatorNotes.0.back: There is one set of estimates in the learner text on purpose: the ILO's Generative AI and jobs, a 2025 update (Gmyrek et al., 20 May 2025, with Poland's NASK, ILO Working Paper 140). It scored nearly 30,000 tasks on how much generative AI could do. 25 percent of jobs worldwide are in occupations with some exposure (34 percent in high-income countries, 11 percent in low-income ones). 3.3 percent are in the most exposed group, mostly clerical jobs such as data entry clerks and typists; in high-income countries this group is 9.6 percent of women's jobs and 3.5 percent of men's. The ILO says these figures reflect potential exposure, an upper limit, not actual employment effects, and expects most jobs to be transformed rather than made redundant, though efficiency gains may still cut labour demand. Other estimates, such as the IMF's (January 2024: nearly 40 percent of jobs exposed to AI overall), cover broader technology and use other methods, so they cannot be set beside the ILO's; the lesson uses only the ILO's. The bank teller example is US data from the 1970s to the 2000s (James Bessen, 2015) and the spreadsheet example is from NPR (2015). Each is one past case, not a prediction for AI.

educatorNotes.1.source: The Speak discussion has no single right answer. Ideas might include retraining the clerk for another task, moving more slowly, or sharing the remaining work; ask who would have to agree (the employer, the workers, a union or the government), which links to the ILO's point about talks between them. A teacher could add a local example of a tool that changed work, without asking about anyone's own job.
educatorNotes.1.back: The Speak discussion has no single right answer. Possible ideas: train the clerk for other tasks, make the change more slowly, or share the remaining work. Ask who would need to agree (employer, workers, a union or government), which links to the ILO's point about talks between these parties. Teachers might add local examples of tools changing jobs, without asking about anyone's own job.
